## Introduction {#sec-apE-intro-en}

@sec-07-http-en gives a web application programmer what they need to
know about the `HTTP` protocol to understand the rest of this book: what
the `GET` and `POST` methods are, how a request reaches a virtual
resource, how PHP receives that data through the superglobals, and how
a site keeps track of a reader's state through *cookies* and sessions,
despite `HTTP` being, by nature, *stateless*. This appendix goes deeper
into this subject beyond what is strictly necessary to develop web
applications, much as a painter does not need to know how to make their
own paint to paint a picture, but benefits from understanding how it is
made. Here, for whoever wants that deeper dive, is the exact syntax of
`GET` and `POST` messages, other common headers, the strategies
*browsers* use to manage connections, and the complete set of *cookie*
attributes.

## The Exact Syntax of HTTP Messages {#sec-apE-messages-en}

@sec-07-request-message-en presents the generic structure of an `HTTP`
message. It is worth seeing, in detail, what each of its parts contains
in the concrete case of a `GET` or `POST` request.

### The GET Request {#sec-apE-get-en}

The *link* to a Contraponto category's articles, seen in
@sec-07-get-en,

```html
<a href="contraponto.pt/artigos.php?categoria=Cultura">Cultura</a>
```

when clicked, results in the following `GET` message:

```bash
GET /artigos.php?categoria=Cultura HTTP/1.1
Host: contraponto.pt
```

`GET` is the method, `/artigos.php?categoria=Cultura` is the requested
resource, and `HTTP/1.1` is the protocol version in use. The `Host`
header indicates which server the request is intended for, essential
when the same IP address hosts several different domains. The `GET`
message has no body, because there is no need to send additional data
to the server, only to request a resource.

Because it changes nothing on the server, the `GET` message is
considered **safe**. This is a convention of the protocol, not a
technical guarantee: a poorly designed server can, technically, change
data in response to a `GET`, but doing so violates the behaviour
expected by any HTTP client, and is considered bad practice.

`GET` can also be used in an HTML form context, as long as the goal is
not to change information on the server, only to obtain a result, as in
a search:

```html
<form action="/pesquisa" method="GET">
    <label for="term">Procurar:</label>
    <input id="term" name="term" type="text" />
    <input type="submit" value="Procurar!" />
</form>
```

When this form is submitted with the term "jornalismo", the *browser*
generates the following message:

```bash
GET /pesquisa?term=jornalismo HTTP/1.1
Host: contraponto.pt
```

Note how the form data appears directly in the URL, after the `?`, in
the `key=value` format, exactly as in the category *link*.

### The POST Request {#sec-apE-post-en}

Contraponto's comment form, referred to in @sec-07-post-en, typically
has this form:

```html
<form action="/comentar.php" method="POST">
    <label for="nome">Nome</label>
    <input id="nome" name="nome" type="text" />
    <label for="texto">Comentário</label>
    <textarea id="texto" name="texto"></textarea>
    <input type="submit" value="Comentar" />
</form>
```

Which, when submitted, results in the following message:

```bash
POST /comentar.php HTTP/1.1
Host: contraponto.pt

nome=Rita&texto=Excelente+artigo%21
```

Unlike `GET`, the data goes in the body of the message, not in the URL.
Notice how the `key=value` format is preserved, but now in the body,
and how special characters in the text (such as `!`) appear encoded
(`%21`), a rule called *URL encoding*, necessary because the body of an
`HTTP` message can only contain a restricted set of characters.

## HTTP Headers {#sec-apE-headers-en}

@sec-07-headers-en presents the `Host` header, the only mandatory one
in a request. Another common header is `Accept`, which tells the server
what content types (`MIME` formats) the *browser* prefers to receive in
the response, in order of preference, indicated by a quality value `q`
between 0 and 1 (the default value is 1, maximum preference):

```bash
GET /artigos.php?categoria=Cultura HTTP/1.1
Host: contraponto.pt
Accept: text/html, application/xhtml+xml, application/xml;q=0.9, */*;q=0.8
```

In this example, the *browser* prefers `HTML`, accepts `XML` with a
slightly lower preference, and accepts any other content type (`*/*`)
only as a last resort.

## Browser Connection Management {#sec-apE-connections-en}

@sec-07-stateless-en explains that each `HTTP` request is, in itself,
independent of all the others, and that a single page normally requires
several requests, one for each resource. To ease this cost, *browsers*
rely on different connection-management strategies:

- **Parallel connections**: on detecting several resources on a page,
  the *browser* opens several connections at once to load them faster,
  one for the HTML, another for the CSS, another for the JavaScript,
  and so on. The number of parallel connections is limited, because
  each additional connection increases the load on the server, which,
  beyond a certain point, can make the page load more slowly instead of
  faster;
- **Persistent connections**: instead of closing the *socket* right
  after each response, the server keeps it open for several successive
  requests. `Apache`, by default, keeps a persistent connection open for
  5 seconds of inactivity before closing it. This period also has to be
  limited for security reasons, to prevent denial-of-service attacks
  (*DoS*), in which an attacker deliberately keeps many connections open
  at once, preventing the server from handling legitimate requests;
- **Back-to-back connections**: since HTTP/1.1, a client can send
  several requests in a row, over the same connection, without waiting
  for the response to each one before sending the next, further
  reducing the total load time of a page with many resources.

## The Attributes of a Cookie {#sec-apE-cookies-en}

@sec-07-cookies-en presents the essentials about *cookies*: a small
piece of information the server asks the *browser* to store and resend
with each following request. *Cookies* are defined, in detail, in the
`RFC 6265` standard, *HTTP State Management Mechanism*.

A server can set several *cookies* at the same time, each with its own
meaning, for example a session identifier and the reader's preferred
language:

```bash
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: sessao=31d4d96e407aad42; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly
Set-Cookie: lang=pt-PT; Path=/; Domain=contraponto.pt
```

A *cookie* set by the server can include several attributes, besides
the name-value pair:

- **`Expires`** or **`Max-Age`**: define when the *cookie* should
  expire (a concrete date, or a number of seconds, respectively); if
  both are set, `Max-Age` takes precedence. With neither of the two,
  the *cookie* expires when the *browser* is closed;
- **`Domain`** and **`Path`**: restrict which *host* and which folder
  on the server the *cookie* is sent to;
- **`Secure`**: the *browser* only sends this *cookie* over a secure
  channel, `HTTPS`;
- **`HttpOnly`**: an important protection against *XSS* attacks, a
  subject explored further in @sec-09-custom-code-en; the *cookie* is
  only exchanged between *browser* and server, without being accessible
  to client-side JavaScript code.

To delete a *cookie*, the server resends it with an expiry date already
in the past; from that point on, the *browser* stops including it in
following requests. Note also that *cookies* are limited to 4kB of
information each. In PHP, a *cookie* is created with the `setcookie()`
function, which accepts all of these attributes as parameters:

```php
<?php
setcookie(
    "utilizador",   // nome
    "joao",         // valor
    time() + 3600,  // expira em 1 hora
    "/",            // path
    "",             // domain
    true,           // secure
    true            // httponly
);
```
